title: Grid dots can reveal a polygon's area
body: Draw a simple polygon whose corners are on an evenly spaced square grid. Pick's theorem gives its area in grid squares by adding the number of interior dots and half the boundary dots, then subtracting one.
takeaway: Even a crooked outline can be measured by counting points instead of slicing it into triangles.
visual: an irregular polygon made of fine thread stretched around pegs on a square grid

title: Multiplying 142857 can rotate its digits
body: The decimal for one seventh repeats 142857. Multiply that six-digit block by any whole number from 1 to 6 and the digits stay in the same circular order. For example, twice 142857 is 285714.
takeaway: A repeating decimal can carry a pattern you can see only after treating its ends as joined.
visual: six beads of different shades strung around a ring on a dark surface

title: Every convex polyhedron has the same counting shortcut
body: Count a convex solid's corners and faces, then subtract its edges. The answer is always 2. A cube gives eight corners plus six faces minus 12 edges, and a tetrahedron gives four plus four minus six.
takeaway: The count exposes a property shared by shapes that look very different.
visual: a wireframe cube beside a small wireframe tetrahedron on a plain surface

title: Any finite list of primes must be incomplete
body: Multiply all the primes on a finite list and add one. Dividing the result by any prime on that list leaves a remainder of one, so the new number must have a prime factor that the list missed.
takeaway: You can prove there is no largest prime without having to find a particular next prime.
visual: a row of small stone blocks receding into darkness with space for one more
